title: Diagonalization, similarity, and powers of a matrix
lead: This section turns the picture of a matrix seen in a basis of eigenvectors into algebra: when a matrix can be written in terms of a diagonal matrix, what that factorization says about its powers, and the broader notion of similarity, which relates a matrix with complex eigenvalues to a rotation and a scaling.
summary_html:
Our goal in this section has been to use the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix $A$ to relate $A$ to a simpler matrix.

  • We said that $A$ is diagonalizable if we can write $A = PDP^{-1}$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. The columns of $P$ consist of eigenvectors of $A$ and the diagonal entries of $D$ are the associated eigenvalues.
  • An $n\times n$ matrix $A$ is diagonalizable if and only if there is a basis of ${\mathbb R}^n$ consisting of eigenvectors of $A$.
  • We said that $A$ and $B$ are similar if there is an invertible matrix $P$ such that $A=PBP^{-1}$. In this case, $A^k = PB^kP^{-1}$.
  • If $A$ is a $2\times2$ matrix with complex eigenvalue $\lambda = a+bi$, then $A$ is similar to $C = \left[\begin{array}{rr} a & -b \\ b & a \\ \end{array} \right]$. Writing the point $(a,b)$ in polar coordinates $r$ and $\theta$, we see that $C$ rotates vectors through an angle $\theta$ and scales them by a factor of $r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.

exercises.prompt:
In this preview activity, we will review some familiar properties about matrix multiplication that appear in this section.

  1. Remember that matrix-vector multiplication constructs linear combinations of the columns of the matrix. For instance, if $A = \begin{bmatrix} {\mathbf a}_1 & {\mathbf a}_2 \end{bmatrix}$, express the product $A\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -3 \end{array}\right]$ in terms of ${\mathbf a}_1$ and ${\mathbf a}_2$.
  2. What is the product $A\left[\begin{array}{r}4 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$ in terms of ${\mathbf a}_1$ and ${\mathbf a}_2$?
  3. Next, remember how matrix-matrix multiplication is defined. Suppose that we have matrices $A$ and $B$ and that $B = \begin{bmatrix} {\mathbf b}_1 & {\mathbf b}_2 \end{bmatrix}$. How can we express the matrix product $AB$ in terms of the columns of $B$?
  4. Suppose that $A$ is a matrix having eigenvectors ${\mathbf v}_1$ and ${\mathbf v}_2$ with associated eigenvalues $\lambda_1 = 4$ and $\lambda_2 = -1$. Express the product $A(2{\mathbf v}_1+3{\mathbf v}_2)$ in terms of ${\mathbf v}_1$ and ${\mathbf v}_2$.

  5. Suppose that $A$ is the matrix from the previous part and that $P=\begin{bmatrix} {\mathbf v}_1 & {\mathbf v}_2 \end{bmatrix}$. What is the matrix product

    $$ AP = A\begin{bmatrix} {\mathbf v}_1 & {\mathbf v}_2 \end{bmatrix}? $$

answer.solution:
Solution.

  1. $A\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -3 \end{array}\right] = 2{\mathbf a}_1 - 3{\mathbf a}_2$.
  2. $A\left[\begin{array}{r}4 \\ 0 \end{array}\right] = 4{\mathbf a}_1$.
  3. $AB = \begin{bmatrix} A{\mathbf b}_1 & A{\mathbf b}_2 \end{bmatrix}$.
  4. $A(2{\mathbf v}_1 + 3{\mathbf v}_2) = 8{\mathbf v}_1 - 3{\mathbf v}_2$.
  5. $AP = \begin{bmatrix} A{\mathbf v}_1 & A{\mathbf v}_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4{\mathbf v}_1 & -{\mathbf v}_2 \end{bmatrix}$.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that $A$ is a $2\times2$ matrix having eigenvectors ${\mathbf v}_1$ and ${\mathbf v}_2$ with associated eigenvalues $\lambda_1=3$ and $\lambda_2 = -6$. Because the eigenvalues are real and distinct, we know by Proposition 4.2.9 that these eigenvectors form a basis of ${\mathbb R}^2$.

  1. What are the products $A{\mathbf v}_1$ and $A{\mathbf v}_2$ in terms of ${\mathbf v}_1$ and ${\mathbf v}_2$?
  2. If we form the matrix $P = \begin{bmatrix} {\mathbf v}_1 & {\mathbf v}_2 \end{bmatrix}$, what is the product $AP$ in terms of ${\mathbf v}_1$ and ${\mathbf v}_2$?
  3. Use the eigenvalues to form the diagonal matrix $D = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -6 \end{bmatrix}$ and determine the product $PD$ in terms of ${\mathbf v}_1$ and ${\mathbf v}_2$.
  4. The results from the previous two parts of this activity demonstrate that $AP=PD$. Using the fact that the eigenvectors ${\mathbf v}_1$ and ${\mathbf v}_2$ form a basis of ${\mathbb R}^2$, explain why $P$ is invertible and that we must have $A=PDP^{-1}$.
  5. Suppose that $A=\begin{bmatrix} -3 & 6 \\ 3 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}$. Verify that ${\mathbf v}_1=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ and ${\mathbf v}_2=\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -1 \end{array}\right]$ are eigenvectors of $A$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1 = 3$ and $\lambda_2=-6$.

  6. Use the Sage cell below to define the matrices $P$ and $D$ and then verify that $A=PDP^{-1}$.

    # enter the matrices P and D below
P =
D =
P*D*P.inverse()

answer.solution:
Solution.

  1. We have $A{\mathbf v}_1=3{\mathbf v}_1$ and $A{\mathbf v}_2 = -6{\mathbf v}_2$.
  2. $AP = \begin{bmatrix} A{\mathbf v}_1 & A{\mathbf v}_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3{\mathbf v}_1 & -6{\mathbf v}_2 \end{bmatrix}$.
  3. $PD = \begin{bmatrix} {\mathbf v}_1 & {\mathbf v}_2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\\ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3{\mathbf v}_1 & -6{\mathbf v}_2 \end{bmatrix}$. Comparing the result of this part of the activity to the previous, we see that $AP = PD$.
  4. Since the eigenvectors form a basis, the columns of $P$ are linearly independent and their span is ${\mathbb R}^2$. This guarantees that $P$ is invertible. Multiplying the equation $AP=PD$ on the right by $P^{-1}$ gives $APP^{-1} = A = PDP^{-1}$.

The rest of the activity can be verified using Sage.

exercises.prompt:
1. Find a diagonalization of $A$, if one exists, when

    $$ A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 3 & -2 \\ 6 & -5 \\ \end{array}\right]. $$

  2. Can the diagonal matrix

    $$ A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 \\ \end{array}\right] $$

    be diagonalized? If so, explain how to find the matrices $P$ and $D$.

  3. Find a diagonalization of $A$, if one exists, when

    $$ A = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -3 \\ \end{array}\right]. $$

  4. Find a diagonalization of $A$, if one exists, when

    $$ A = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & -3 \\ \end{array}\right]. $$

  5. Suppose that $A=PDP^{-1}$ where

    $$ D = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ \end{array}\right],\qquad P = \left[\begin{array}{cc} {\mathbf v}_2 & {\mathbf v}_1 \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 \\ \end{array}\right]. $$
    1. Explain why $A$ is invertible.
    2. Find a diagonalization of $A^{-1}$.
    3. Find a diagonalization of $A^3$.

answer.solution:
Solution.

  1. We find that $A$ has eigenvectors ${\mathbf v}_1=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ with associated eigenvalue $\lambda_1=1$ and ${\mathbf v}_2=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 3 \end{array}\right]$ with associated eigenvalue $\lambda_2=-3$. We then have $P=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ \end{array}\right]$ and $D=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 \\ \end{array}\right]$.
  2. Yes. We know that the eigenvectors are ${\mathbf v}_1=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$ with associated eigenvalue $\lambda_1=2$ and ${\mathbf v}_2=\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ with associated eigenvalue $\lambda_2=-5$. Therefore, $P = \left[\begin{array}{rr}{\mathbf v}_1 & {\mathbf v}_2 \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right]=I$ and $D=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 \\ \end{array}\right]=A$. This shows that the diagonalization is $A=IAI^{-1}$; that is, since $A$ is already diagonal, it is diagonalized by the identity matrix.

  3. We find eigenvectors ${\mathbf v}_1=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$, ${\mathbf v}_2=\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$, and ${\mathbf v}_3=\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ with associated eigenvalues $\lambda_1=-2$, $\lambda_2=-3$, and $\lambda_3=-3$. Therefore, $A = PDP^{-1}$ where

    $$ P = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right], D = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3 \\ \end{array}\right]\text{.} $$
  4. Once again, we see that $\lambda=-2$ is an eigenvalue with multiplicity one and $\lambda=-3$ is an eigenvalue with multiplicity two. However, $\dim E_{-3} = 1$ so we are not able to find a basis for ${\mathbb R}^3$ consisting of eigenvalues of $A$. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.

  5. If $A=PDP^{-1}$,

    1. $A$ is invertible since $\det A = \det D = -3$.
    2. We know that ${\mathbf v}_1$ and ${\mathbf v}_2$ are eigenvectors of $A$ with associated eigenvalues $\lambda_1=3$ and $\lambda_2=-1$. If ${\mathbf v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ with associated eigenvalue $\lambda$, then ${\mathbf v}$ is an eigenvector of $A^{-1}$ with associated eigenvalue $\frac1{\lambda}$. Therefore, $A^{-1} = PEP^{-1}$ where $E = \left[\begin{array}{rr} \frac13 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ \end{array}\right]$.
    3. We have $A^3=PFP^{-1}$ where $F=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 27 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ \end{array}\right]$.

exercises.prompt:
1. Let’s begin with the diagonal matrix

    $$ D = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ \end{array}\right]. $$

    Find the powers $D^2$, $D^3$, and $D^4$. What is $D^k$ for a general value of $k$?

  2. Suppose that $A$ is a matrix with eigenvector ${\mathbf v}$ and associated eigenvalue $\lambda$; that is, $A{\mathbf v} = \lambda{\mathbf v}$. By considering $A^2{\mathbf v}$, explain why ${\mathbf v}$ is also an eigenvector of $A^2$ with eigenvalue $\lambda^2$.

  3. Suppose that $A= PDP^{-1}$ where

    $$ D = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ \end{array}\right]. $$

    Remembering that the columns of $P$ are eigenvectors of $A$, explain why $A^2$ is diagonalizable and find a diagonalization in terms of $P$ and $D$.

  4. Give another explanation of the diagonalizability of $A^2$ by writing

    $$ A^2 = (PDP^{-1})(PDP^{-1}) = PD(P^{-1}P)DP^{-1}. $$
  5. In the same way, find a diagonalization of $A^3$, $A^4$, and $A^k$.
  6. Suppose that $A$ is a diagonalizable $2\times2$ matrix with eigenvalues $\lambda_1 = 0.5$ and $\lambda_2=0.1$. What happens to $A^k$ as $k$ becomes very large?

answer.solution:
Solution.

  1. We have

    $$ D^2=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right], D^3=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 8 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ \end{array}\right], \ldots, D^k=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 2^k & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^k \\ \end{array}\right]\text{.} $$
  2. We know that $A^2{\mathbf v} = \lambda A{\mathbf v} = \lambda^2{\mathbf v}$ so that ${\mathbf v}$ is also an eigenvector of $A^2$ with associated eigenvalue $\lambda^2$.
  3. Since eigenvectors of $A$ are also eigenvectors of $A^2$, we can use the matrix $P$ to diagonalize $A^2$. The eigenvalues are squared, however, so we have $A^2=PEP^{-1}$ where $E=D^2=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right]$.

  4. We can also see this by noting that

    $$ \begin{aligned} A^2 & = (PDP^{-1})(PDP^{-1}) = PD(P^{-1}P)DP^{-1} \\ & = PDIDP^{-1} = PD^2P^{-1}\text{.}\\ \end{aligned} $$
  5. $A^3=PD^3P^{-1}$, $A^4=PD^4P^{-1}$, and $A^k=PD^kP^{-1}$.
  6. We can write $A=PDP^{-1}$ where $D=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.1 \\ \end{array}\right]$. Therefore, $A^k=PD^kP^{-1}$ where $D^k=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 0.5^k & 0 \\ 0 & 0.1^k \\ \end{array}\right]$. As $k$ becomes very large, $0.5^k$ and $0.1^k$ become very close to zero. Hence $D^k$ and $A^k$ become very close to the zero matrix.

exercises.prompt:
We begin by rewriting $C$ in terms of $r$ and $\theta$ and noting that

$$ C = \left[\begin{array}{rr} a & -b \\ b & a \\ \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{rr} r\cos\theta & -r\sin\theta \\ r\sin\theta & r\cos\theta \\ \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{rr} r & 0 \\ 0 & r \\ \end{array}\right] \left[\begin{array}{rr} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \\ \end{array}\right]. $$
  1. Explain why $C$ has the geometric effect of rotating vectors by $\theta$ and scaling them by a factor of $r$.

  2. Let’s now consider the matrix

    $$ A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} -2 & 2 \\ -5 & 4 \\ \end{array}\right] $$

    whose eigenvalues are $\lambda_1 = 1+i$ and $\lambda_2 = 1-i$. We will choose to focus on one of the eigenvalues $\lambda_1 = a+bi= 1+i.$

    Form the matrix $C$ using these values of $a$ and $b$. Then rewrite the point $(a,b)$ in polar coordinates by identifying the values of $r$ and $\theta$. Explain the geometric effect of multiplying vectors by $C$.

  3. Suppose that $P=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right]$. Verify that $A = PCP^{-1}$.

    C =
P =
P*C*P.inverse()
  4. Explain why $A^k = PC^kP^{-1}$.
  5. We formed the matrix $C$ by choosing the eigenvalue $\lambda_1=1+i$. Suppose we had instead chosen $\lambda_2 = 1-i$. Form the matrix $C'$ and use polar coordinates to describe the geometric effect of $C'$.
  6. Using the matrix $P' = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 \\ \end{array}\right]$, show that $A = P'C'P'^{-1}$.

answer.solution:
Solution.

  1. The matrix $S=\left[\begin{array}{rr} r & 0 \\ 0 & r \\ \end{array}\right]$ has the geometric effect of scaling vectors uniformly by a factor of $r$ while the matrix $R=\left[\begin{array}{rr} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \\ \end{array}\right]$ rotates vectors by $\theta$.
  2. We have $a=b=1$ so we form the matrix $C=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{rr} \sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ \end{array}\right] \left[\begin{array}{rr} \cos(45^\circ) & -\sin(45^\circ) \\ \sin(45^\circ) & \cos(45^\circ) \\ \end{array}\right]$. This shows that $C$ will scale vectors by a factor of $\sqrt2$ while rotating them by $45^\circ$.
  3. Sage will verify this relationship.
  4. As we saw earlier, we have $A^2 = (PCP^{-1})(PCP^{-1}) = PC^2P^{-1}$ and hence $A^k = PC^kP^{-1}$.
  5. We have $a=1$ and $b=-1$ so we form the matrix $C'=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{rr} \sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ \end{array}\right] \left[\begin{array}{rr} \cos(-45^\circ) & -\sin(-45^\circ) \\ \sin(-45^\circ) & \cos(-45^\circ) \\ \end{array}\right]$. This shows that $C$ will scale vectors by a factor of $\sqrt2$ while rotating them by $-45^\circ$.

exercises.prompt:
Determine whether the following matrices are diagonalizable. If so, find matrices $D$ and $P$ such that $A=PDP^{-1}$.

  1. $A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right]$.
  2. $A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} -1 & 1 \\ -1 & -3 \\ \end{array}\right]$.
  3. $A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 3 & -4 \\ 2 & -1 \\ \end{array}\right]$.
  4. $A = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ \end{array}\right]$.
  5. $A = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right]$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $P = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right]$ and $D=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 \\ \end{array}\right]$
  2. $A$ is not diagonalizable.
  3. $A$ is not diagonalizable.
  4. $P = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 9 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 6 & 0 \\ -2 & -1 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right]$ and $D = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ \end{array}\right]$
  5. $P = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right]$ and $D = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ \end{array}\right]$

Solution.

  1. We find that ${\mathbf v}_1=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]$ is an eigenvector with associated eigenvalue $\lambda_1=2$ as is ${\mathbf v}_2=\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ with associated eigenvalue $\lambda_2=-3$. Therefore, we have $A=PDP^{-1}$ where

    $$ P = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right], D=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 \\ \end{array}\right]\text{.} $$
  2. We see that $\lambda=-2$ is an eigenvalue having multiplicity two. However, $\dim E_{-2} = 1$ so we cannot find a basis for ${\mathbb R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors of $A$. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.
  3. We see that $A$ has complex eigenvalues $\lambda=1\pm 2i$ so it is not diagonalizable in the form $A=PDP^{-1}$ for a diagonal matrix $D$.

  4. The matrix $A$ has three distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_1=1$, $\lambda_2=-2$, and $\lambda_3=4$ with associated eigenvectors ${\mathbf v}_1=\left[\begin{array}{r}9 \\ 6 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]$, ${\mathbf v}_2=\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 6 \\ -1 \end{array}\right]$, and ${\mathbf v}_3=\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$. This shows us that $A=PDP^{-1}$ where

    $$ P = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 9 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & 6 & 0 \\ -2 & -1 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right], D = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ \end{array}\right]\text{.} $$

  5. We have an eigenvalue $\lambda=-1$ having multiplicity two, but its eigenspace has dimension two so $A$ is diagonalizable. In particular, we choose

    $$ P = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right], D = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ \end{array}\right] $$

    and have $A=PDP^{-1}$.

exercises.prompt:
Determine whether the following matrices have complex eigenvalues. If so, find the matrix $C$ such that $A = PCP^{-1}$.

  1. $A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right]$.
  2. $A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} -1 & 1 \\ -1 & -3 \\ \end{array}\right]$.
  3. $A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 3 & -4 \\ 2 & -1 \\ \end{array}\right]$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. There are two real eigenvalues.
  2. There is a single real eigenvalue.
  3. $C=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right]$ or $C=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right]$.

Solution.

  1. We have two real eigenvalues $\lambda=2, -3$.
  2. We have a single real eigenvalue $\lambda=-2$.
  3. We have complex eigenvalues $\lambda=1\pm2i$ so we can choose $C=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right]$ or $C=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right]$.

exercises.prompt:
Determine whether the following statements are true or false and provide a justification for your response.

  1. If $A$ is invertible, then $A$ is diagonalizable.
  2. If $A$ and $B$ are similar and $A$ is invertible, then $B$ is also invertible.
  3. If $A$ is a diagonalizable $n\times n$ matrix, then there is a basis of ${\mathbb R}^n$ consisting of eigenvectors of $A$.
  4. If $A$ is diagonalizable, then $A^{10}$ is also diagonalizable.
  5. If $A$ is diagonalizable, then $A$ is invertible.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. False
  2. True
  3. True
  4. True
  5. False

Solution.

  1. False. A matrix can be invertible without us being able to form a basis consisting of eigenvectors. An example is $\left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \\ \end{array}\right]$.
  2. True. If $A$ and $B$ are similar, then $A=PBP^{-1}$ so that $\det A = \det B$. If $A$ is invertible, we know that $\det A \neq 0$, which also tells us that $\det B\neq 0$ and hence that $B$ is invertible.
  3. True. If $A=PDP^{-1}$, then the columns of $P$ are eigenvectors of $A$ that form a basis for ${\mathbb R}^n$.
  4. True. If $A=PDP^{-1}$, then $A^{10}=PD^{10}P^{-1}$.
  5. False. It is possible that $A$ has eigenvalue $\lambda=0$, which would imply that $A$ is not invertible.

exercises.prompt:
Provide a justification for your response to the following questions.

  1. If $A$ is a $3\times3$ matrix having eigenvalues $\lambda = 2, 3, -4$, can you guarantee that $A$ is diagonalizable?
  2. If $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix with a complex eigenvalue, can you guarantee that $A$ is diagonalizable?
  3. If $A$ is similar to the matrix $B = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} -5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \\ \end{array}\right]$, is $A$ diagonalizable?
  4. What can you say about a matrix that is similar to the identity matrix?
  5. If $A$ is a diagonalizable $2\times2$ matrix with a single eigenvalue $\lambda = 4$, what is $A$?

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. Yes
  2. No
  3. Yes
  4. Only the identity
  5. $A=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ \end{array}\right]$.

Solution.

  1. Yes. If $A$ has $3$ real and distinct eigenvalues, then there is a basis of ${\mathbb R}^3$ consisting of eigenvectors of $A$. Therefore, $A$ is diagonalizable.
  2. No. We can write $A=PCP^{-1}$ where $C=\left[\begin{array}{rr} a & -b \\ b & a \\ \end{array}\right]$, but $A$ is not diagonalizable.
  3. Yes. Since $B$ is diagonal and $A=PBP^{-1}$, then $A$ is diagonalizable.
  4. Only the identity because $A=PIP^{-1} = PP^{-1} = I$.
  5. $A=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ \end{array}\right]$. If we denote $D=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ \end{array}\right]=4I$, then $A=PDP^{-1}=P4IP^{-1} = 4I = D$.

exercises.prompt:
Describe geometric effect that the following matrices have on ${\mathbb R}^2$:

  1. $A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \\ \end{array}\right]$
  2. $A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 \\ \end{array}\right]$
  3. $A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 3 & -6 \\ 6 & 3 \\ \end{array}\right]$
  4. $A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \\ \end{array}\right]$
  5. $A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right]$

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. Multiplying by $A$ uniformly stretches vectors by a factor of $2$.
  2. This is a shear so that vectors are stretched and then pushed horizontally.
  3. We write $(a,b) = (3,6) = (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)$ where $r=3\sqrt{5}$ and $\theta = \arctan(2)$. Therefore, $A$ will stretch vectors by a factor of $3\sqrt{5}$ and rotate them by $\theta\approx 63.4^\circ$.
  4. Vectors are stretched in the horizontal direction by a factor of $4$ and stretched vertically by a factor of $2$ before being reflected in the horizontal axis.
  5. This matrix has eigenvectors ${\mathbf v}_1=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ with associated eigenvalue $\lambda_1=4$ and ${\mathbf v}_2=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ with $\lambda_2=-2$. Therefore, $A$ stretches vectors by a factor of $4$ in the direction of ${\mathbf v}_1$ and a factor of $2$ in the direction of ${\mathbf v}_1$ before reflecting in the line defined by ${\mathbf v}_1$.

Solution.

  1. Multiplying by $A$ uniformly stretches vectors by a factor of $2$.
  2. This is a shear so that vectors are stretched and then pushed horizontally.
  3. We write $(a,b) = (3,6) = (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)$ where $r=3\sqrt{5}$ and $\theta = \arctan(2)$. Therefore, $A$ will stretch vectors by a factor of $3\sqrt{5}$ and rotate them by $\theta\approx 63.4^\circ$.
  4. Vectors are stretched in the horizontal direction by a factor of $4$ and stretched vertically by a factor of $2$ before being reflected in the horizontal axis.

This matrix has eigenvectors ${\mathbf v}_1=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ with associated eigenvalue $\lambda_1=4$ and ${\mathbf v}_2=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ with $\lambda_2=-2$. exercises.prompt:
We say that $A$ is similar to $B$ if there is a matrix $P$ such that $A = PBP^{-1}$.

  1. If $A$ is similar to $B$, explain why $B$ is similar to $A$.
  2. If $A$ is similar to $B$ and $B$ is similar to $C$, explain why $A$ is similar to $C$.
  3. If $A$ is similar to $B$ and $B$ is diagonalizable, explain why $A$ is diagonalizable.
  4. If $A$ and $B$ are similar, explain why $A$ and $B$ have the same characteristic polynomial; that is, explain why $\det(A-\lambda I) = \det(B-\lambda I)$.
  5. If $A$ and $B$ are similar, explain why $A$ and $B$ have the same eigenvalues.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. If $A=PBP^{-1}$, then $B=P^{-1}AP$. If we call $Q=P^{-1}$, then $B=QAQ^{-1}$, which shows that $B$ is similar to $A$.
  2. If $A=PBP^{-1}$ and $B=QCQ^{-1}$, then $A=PQCP^{-1}Q^{-1} = (PQ)C(PQ)^{-1}$, which shows that $A$ is similar to $C$.
  3. If $B$ is diagonalizable, then it is similar to a diagonal matrix $D$. Since $A$ is similar to $B$ and $B$ is similar to $D$, we know that $A$ is also similar to $D$ so that $A$ is diagonalizable.

  4. If $A=PBP^{-1}$, then

    $$ \begin{aligned} \det(A-\lambda I) & = \det(PBP^{-1}-\lambda PP^{-1}) \\ & = \det[P(B-\lambda I)P^{-1}] \\ & = \det(B-\lambda I)\text{.} \\ \end{aligned} $$
  5. The eigenvalues of a matrix are the roots of its characteristic polynomial. If $A$ and $B$ are similar, then they have the same characteristic polynomial and hence the same eigenvalues.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that $A = PDP^{-1}$ where

$$ D = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ \end{array}\right],\qquad P = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ \end{array}\right]. $$
  1. Explain the geometric effect that $D$ has on vectors in ${\mathbb R}^2$.
  2. Explain the geometric effect that $A$ has on vectors in ${\mathbb R}^2$.
  3. What can you say about $A^2$ and other powers of $A$?
  4. Is $A$ invertible?

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. The matrix $D$ projects vectors onto the horizontal axis.
  2. $A$ projects vectors onto the line defined by the eigenvector $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$.
  3. $A^k=A$.
  4. No

Solution.

  1. The matrix $D$ projects vectors onto the horizontal axis; that is, it produces the shadow of a vector on the horizontal axis from a flashlight shining down the vertical axis.
  2. $A$ projects vectors onto the line defined by the eigenvector $\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$.
  3. Since $A=PDP^{-1}$ and $D^2 = D$, we have $A^2 = PD^2P^{-1} = PDP^{-1} = A$. That is, $A^2 = A$ and $A^k=A$.
  4. $A$ is not invertible because $\lambda=0$ is an eigenvalue.

exercises.prompt:
When $A$ is a $2\times2$ matrix with a complex eigenvalue $\lambda = a+bi$, we have said that there is a matrix $P$ such that $A=PCP^{-1}$ where $C=\left[\begin{array}{rr} a & -b \\ b & a \\ \end{array}\right]$. In this exercise, we will learn how to find the matrix $P$. As an example, we will consider the matrix $A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 & 2 \\ -1 & 4 \\ \end{array}\right]$.

  1. Show that the eigenvalues of $A$ are complex.
  2. Choose one of the complex eigenvalues $\lambda=a+bi$ and construct the usual matrix $C$.
  3. Using the same eigenvalue, we will find an eigenvector ${\mathbf v}$ where the entries of ${\mathbf v}$ are complex numbers. As always, we will describe $\text{Nul}(A-\lambda I)$ by constructing the matrix $A-\lambda I$ and finding its reduced row echelon form. In doing so, we will necessarily need to use complex arithmetic.
  4. We have now found a complex eigenvector ${\mathbf v}$. Write ${\mathbf v} = {\mathbf v}_1 - i {\mathbf v}_2$ to identify vectors ${\mathbf v}_1$ and ${\mathbf v}_2$ having real entries.
  5. Construct the matrix $P = \left[\begin{array}{rr} {\mathbf v}_1 & {\mathbf v}_2 \end{array}\right]$ and verify that $A=PCP^{-1}$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\lambda = 3\pm i$.
  2. If $\lambda=3+i$, then $C=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 3 & -1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ \end{array}\right]$.
  3. ${\mathbf v} = \left[\begin{array}{r}1-i \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$
  4. ${\mathbf v}_1=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ and ${\mathbf v}_2=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$.
  5. $P = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ \end{array}\right]$

Solution.

  1. The eigenvalues are $\lambda = 3\pm i$.
  2. We will choose $\lambda=3+i$ so that $C=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 3 & -1 \\ 1 & 3 \\ \end{array}\right]$.

  3. Construct the matrix

    $$ A-(3+i)I = \left[\begin{array}{rr} -1-i & 2 \\ -1 & 1-i \\ \end{array}\right] \sim \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & -1+i \\ 0 & 0 \\ \end{array}\right] $$

    so that a basis vector for the null space is ${\mathbf v} = \left[\begin{array}{r}1-i \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.

  4. We have ${\mathbf v}=\left[\begin{array}{r}1-i \\ 1 \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]-i\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$ giving ${\mathbf v}_1=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ and ${\mathbf v}_2=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$.
  5. We let $P = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ \end{array}\right]$ and verify that $A=PCP^{-1}$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

In each case, the vectors are rotated by $90^\circ$. Note that the figures below are draw at different scales.

  1. The vectors are stretched by a factor of 1.4.

  2. The vectors are stretched by a factor of 0.8.

  3. The length of the vectors is unchanged.

exercises.prompt:
For each of the following matrices and vectors, sketch the vector ${\mathbf x}$ along with $A^k{\mathbf x}$ for $k=1,2,3,4$.

  1. $$ \begin{aligned} A & {}={} \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1.4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.7 \\ \end{array}\right] \\ \\ {\mathbf x} & {}={} \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]\text{.} \end{aligned} $$
  2. $$ \begin{aligned} A & {}={} \left[\begin{array}{rr} 0.6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.9 \\ \end{array}\right] \\ \\ {\mathbf x} & {}={} \left[\begin{array}{r}4 \\ 3 \end{array}\right]\text{.} \end{aligned} $$
  3. $$ \begin{aligned} A & {}={} \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1.2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.4 \\ \end{array}\right] \\ \\ {\mathbf x} & {}={} \left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]\text{.} \end{aligned} $$
  4. $$ \begin{aligned} A & {}={} \left[\begin{array}{rr} 0.95 & 0.25 \\ 0.25 & 0.95 \\ \end{array}\right] \\ \\ {\mathbf x} & {}={} \left[\begin{array}{r}3 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]\text{.} \end{aligned} $$

    Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $A$ to create your sketch.

  5. If $A$ is a $2\times2$ matrix with eigenvalues $\lambda_1=0.7$ and $\lambda_2=0.5$ and ${\mathbf x}$ is any vector, what happens to $A^k{\mathbf x}$ when $k$ becomes very large?

answer.solution:
Answer.

  5. Vectors will be pulled into the origin.

Solution.

  1. Vectors are expanded horizontally and compressed vertically.
  2. Vectors are compressed both horizontally and vertically.
  3. Vectors are expanded both horizontally and vertically.
  4. There are eigenvectors ${\mathbf v}_1=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ with $\lambda_1 = 1.2$ and ${\mathbf v}_2=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ with $\lambda_2=0.7$. Vectors are expanded in the direction of ${\mathbf v}_1$ and compressed in the direction of ${\mathbf v}_2$.
  5. Because both eigenvalues have an absolute value smaller than $1$, vectors will be compressed in the direction of both eigenvectors and hence be pulled into the origin.

footnotes.html: The book prints $\kP = \left[\begin{array}{cc} \kvecvtwo & \kvecvone \end{array}\right]$; the columns it then names, $\kvecvone = \left[\begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ first and $\kvecvtwo = \left[\begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$ second, make it $\kP = \left[\begin{array}{cc} \kvecvone & \kvecvtwo \end{array}\right]$, in the order of the eigenvalues on the diagonal of $\kD$.

The book prints $\kA\kvecvone = \left[\begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kA\kvecvtwo = \left[\begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$; the products are $\kA\kvecvone = \left[\begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 2 \end{array}\right] = 2\kvecvone$ and $\kA\kvecvtwo = \left[\begin{array}{r} -2 \\ -4 \end{array}\right] = -2\kvecvtwo$, which is the check meant.

The book prints $P = \left[\begin{array}{cc} {\mathbf v}_2 & {\mathbf v}_1 \end{array}\right]$; the first column $\left[\begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ is the eigenvector with eigenvalue $3 = \lambda_1$, as the solution uses it, so $P = \left[\begin{array}{cc} {\mathbf v}_1 & {\mathbf v}_2 \end{array}\right]$ is meant, in the order of the eigenvalues on the diagonal of $D$.

The book’s answer prints $P = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \end{array}\right]$; its first column should be the eigenvector ${\mathbf v}_1 = \left[\begin{array}{r} 1 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]$ of the solution, since $A\left[\begin{array}{r} 1 \\ -1 \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{r} 0 \\ -3 \end{array}\right]$ is not a multiple of $\left[\begin{array}{r} 1 \\ -1 \end{array}\right]$: $P = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 \end{array}\right]$.

The book’s answer and solution print “a factor of $2$ in the direction of ${\mathbf v}_1$”; the stretch by $2$, with the reflection, is in the direction of ${\mathbf v}_2 = \left[\begin{array}{r} -1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$, whose eigenvalue is $-2$.
